Abstract
Using acoustic emission (AE) technique to locate the microcracking of rock samples in the process of rock mechanics test is
one of the most efective means to study the spatio-temporal evolution of rock failure. At present, the research on AE source
localization method for layered rock considering anisotropic P-wave velocity is insuficient and the location methods are
usually two-dimensional. This paper first analyses the characteristics of P-wave velocity of layered rocks, and a method for
establishing anisotropic P-wave velocity model of layered rocks is introduced. Then, a three-dimensional AE source locali
zation method for layered rocks is proposed based on the anisotropic P-wave velocity model and simplex algorithm. The
influences of iterative initial value, iterative contraction length, number of iterations and P-wave velocity measurement error
on the positioning accuracy of this method are studied. And selection methods of those iterative parameters are introduced.
Finally, the numerical analysis and true triaxial compression tests for quartz mica schist, quartz schist and black shale are
conducted to verify the high location accuracy and eficiency of the proposed method. Numerical tests show that the aver-
age absolute distance errors of AE location results are less than 1 mm when the P-wave velocity measurement error is less
than 5%, which is much less than that arising from use of the traditional simplex method. And the AE location results are
consistent with the failure modes of the true triaxial compression test rock samples.

Time diference of arrival (TDOA) location method is the
most widely used method to determine the location of AE
sources. Commonly used TDOA location methods include
the least squares algorithm (Fedorow 1974), Geiger location
algorithm (Geiger 1912), and simplex location algorithm
(Nelder and Mead 1965). The location accuracy of simplex
algorithm is higher than that of Geiger location method
(Prugger and Gendzwill 1988). Diferent wave velocities
can be set in each direction when using simplex method,
which is in accord with the actual situation. This direct itera-
tive method is simple in concept, does not require derivative
calculation, avoids matrix inversion, and the iteration con-
verges readily. Most of the widely used AE source location
methods are based on the premise of measuring the average
wave velocity in advance or giving a fixed unknown wave
velocity value (Liu et al. 2015; Dong et al. 2015, 2020; Li
et al. 2021; Zhou et al. 2021). The above methods assume
that the wave velocities of rocks are equal in all directions.
However, for anisotropic layered rocks, due to the presence
of inherent planes of anisotropy, there is a significant dif-
ference in wave velocities in diferent directions. The AE
source location methods based on the isotropic wave veloc-
ity value have poor efect in locating the microfracture of
layered rocks. The inherent planes of anisotropy including
schistosity plane, foliation plane, bedding plane, etc. Within
the scope of this study, they all play a role in influencing
wave velocity of layered rock.

In terms of AE source localization algorithm for aniso-
tropic materials, Zhou et al. (2020) and Yin et al. (2019,
2021) considered the refraction of AE wave at the hetero-
geneous interface, and deduced the velocity model of AE
signal propagation in two-layered or three-layered hetero-
geneous structures based on Snell’s theorem. This method
is based on the idealized heterogeneous interface and is
suitable for materials with a simple layered structure. The
heterogeneous structure of layered rocks is much more com-
plex, it is dificult to generalize by idealized two-layered
or three-layered heterogeneous structure. Based on the grid
search and simplex algorithm, some researchers proposed
AE source location methods for the failure process of ani-
sotropic material (Kundu et al. 2009; Debecker and Ver-
voort 2011; Hajzargerbashi et al. 2011; Zhang et al. 2019,
2020; Wu et al. 2021). The grid search method needs to
divide the whole test object into small grids, calculate the
error of each grid point, and take the point with the small-
est error as the positioning result. When the grid division
is sparse, the accuracy of this method is low, and when the
division is dense, the calculations in this method will be both
complex and onerous. And most of these methods focus on
two-dimensional plate tests or rock uniaxial compression
tests, do not conducted true triaxial experiments to verify
the accuracy of the localization algorithm. In addition, there
are limited researches on the selection method of iterative
parameters (namely, iterative initial value, iterative contrac-
tion length, and number of iterations) in simplex algorithm,
however, these parameters have a significant impact on posi-
tioning accuracy.
In view of this, a method for establishing anisotropic
P-wave velocity model of layered rocks is introduced. And
a three-dimensional layered rock AE source localization
method is proposed based on the anisotropic P-wave velocity
model and simplex algorithm. The influences of iterative
parameters and P-wave velocity measurement error on the
positioning accuracy of this method are studied, selec-
tion methods of those iterative parameters are introduced.
Finally, the location accuracy and computational conveni-
ence of this method are verified through numerical analysis
and true triaxial compression tests.
Anisotropic P‑wave velocity model
of layered rock
Since P-wave propagates fastest in seismic signal phases,
the P-wave in the waveform generated by AE events reaches
the sensor first, the signal can be detected faster, which is
beneficial for real-time monitoring and rapid response.
Due to the strong interference of P-phase aftermath and the
twice-reflected phase, S-wave generation and propagation
are more complicated than P-wave, and S-wave arrival pick-
ing is more dificult than P-wave (Zhu et al. 2018; Li et al.
2023). S-wave usually has more energy and is less afected
by waveform attenuation, therefore, S-wave based position-
ing methods are commonly used for large-scale structures.
However, for a small-size structure AE event excitation,
there usually equipped with three phases, S-wave, reflected
wave and surface wave, which will significantly increase the
complexity of P-wave coda (Shang et al. 2022). Therefore,
it is more appropriate only use P-wave arrival time data for
AE event location for a small-size structure. In this paper,
the arrival time diference of P-wave is used for calculation.

P-wave velocity model of layered rock is introduced, which
is also applicable to other similar types of rock.

Method for establishing anisotropic P‑wave velocity
model of layered rocks
According to the wave equation, when the medium is an
ideal homogeneous material and non-linear effects are
ignored, the mechanical wave velocity in the medium is a
fixed value, which depends on the elastic parameters and
density of the material. For rocks with good homogeneity
and low porosity, it can be approximately considered that the
P-wave velocities are equal in all directions, however, it can
be seen from the above section that the degree of heteroge-
neity and anisotropy of layered rocks is very high. Due to
the presence of foliation planes, the P-wave velocity in rocks
exhibits significant anisotropy, which cannot be ignored.
For this kind of material, it is dificult and unnecessary
to establish the propagation path of P-waves in microscopic
scale: it is dificult to construct its P-wave velocity model
by wave equation and Snell’s theorem, because it is neither
an ideal two-layered or three-layered heterogeneous struc-
ture, nor an ideal transversely isotropic material. In addition,
due to the discreteness between samples, it is inappropriate
to use a unified formula to describe the properties of all
samples.

the angle θ, which is formed between foliation plane and
the connecting line of wave transmitter (or AE source) and

Since the location of the AE source is unknown, to avoid the
influence of human subjectivity on the search direction of the
simplex, the shape of the initial simplex should be a regular
tetrahedron. And the first sensor receiving the AE signal is take
as the center of the regular tetrahedron, which is conducive to
the iteration converging to the global minimum value.
When considering the influence of the iterative initial
value, the selected iterative contraction length is a third of
side length of the tetrahedron and the number of iterations
is one hundred. Due to the real P-wave velocity matrix being
dot multiplied by a random number matrix and the random
number matrix generated each time is diferent, the P-wave
velocity model used in each calculation will be diferent. And
diferent P-wave velocity models will lead to diferent posi-
tioning results. Therefore, in order to avoid the influence of
random number matrix on the location results, a hundred posi-
tioning calculations using diferent random number matrices
are conducted for each AE source in each numerical sample,
and the average value is taken as the positioning result. The
numerical tests are carried out respectively considering that
the distance between the vertices of the initial simplex and
the center point is 2 mm, 5 mm, 10 mm, 15 mm, 20 mm, 25
mm, and 30 mm. The average error of the positioning results
of nine AE sources in each model (the distance between the
positioning results and the actual value) is calculated. The test
results are shown in Fig. 9.
Figure 9 indicates that when the distance between the ver-
tices of the initial simplex and the center point is about 15
mm, the iterative result is stable, and the positioning error is
small. The selection of the iterative initial value is related to
the number and arrangement of AE sensors. According to the
sensor arrangement adopted herein (Fig. 3), the minimum
distance between two sensors is 29.8 mm, therefore, it is sug-
gested that the distance between the vertices of the initial
simplex and the center point is 1/2 of the minimum distance
between any two sensors.

several aspects require optimization and improvement.
1. In addition to bedding planes, loading stress also has

will provide better location results.
2. The method proposed in this article is applicable to lay-
ered rocks with a set of parallel bedding planes. It is
not applicable to rocks with multiple sets of bedding
planes in diferent directions or rocks with folding bed-
ding planes. The influence of these factors should be
considered in future research.
3. Through the AE localization, the location of rock frac-
ture and its evolution process can be determined. By
analyzing the location of AE events and the time series
of AE hit, higher quality forecast for layered rock failure
can be achieved (Zhang and Zhou  2020; Zhang et al.
2023). The relative research can be conducted in the
future.
4. This article mainly studies the AE source localization
method of layered rocks in laboratory rock mechan-
ics tests. The application of the results of this study
in geotechnical projects such as deep tunnels and rock
slopes should be studied in future. The instability of
geotechnical projects is inherently linked to AE activity
within them. When monitorable displacement occurs
on the surface of deep tunnels or rock slopes, micro-
fractures have already taken place within the rock mass.
The failure of layered rock mass is significantly afected
by bedding structure. And the failure location of lay-
ered rock mass is diferent from that of isotropic rock
mass. By deploying AE sensors within the geotechni-
cal projects, it is possible to continuously monitor the
AE signals generated by layered rock fractures in real
time and utilize localization algorithms to determine
the location of the fracture source. This facilitates the
timely identification of potential layered rock fracture
hazards and provides a basis for taking necessary sup-
port and reinforcement measures.
Conclusions
A three-dimensional AE source localization method for
layered rock is proposed based on simplex method and the
established anisotropic P-wave velocity model. The factors
afecting the positioning accuracy of the method are stud-
ied. And the accuracy of the proposed method is verified
by numerical analysis and true triaxial compression test.
The main conclusions are drawn as follows:
1. Due to the presence of foliation planes, the P-wave
velocity of layered rocks exhibits significant anisot-
ropy. A method is proposed to establish the anisotropic
P-wave velocity model of layered rock, which can accu-
rately reflect the anisotropic propagation velocity char-
acteristics of AE signals generated by microfracture in
layered rock;
2. A three-dimensional AE source location method for
layered rock is proposed based on simplex method and
the established anisotropic P-wave velocity model. The
iterative initial value exerts a relatively large influence
on the positioning accuracy of the proposed method,
while the iterative contraction length has relatively lit-
tle efect on the positioning accuracy. When the dis-
tance between the vertices of the initial simplex and the
center point is 1/2 of the minimum distance between
any two sensors and the contraction length is about
1/3 of the original side length of the tetrahedron, the
positioning efect is relatively good and stable;
3. For layered rocks with high anisotropy and heteroge-
neity, the location accuracy of the proposed method is
much higher than that of the traditional method (iso-
tropic P-wave velocity simplex method). In addition,
this method allows rapid convergence, as the number
of iterations increases, the localization error initially
decreases rapidly, but the rate of decrease slows down
as iterations continue. When the number of iterations
reaches 100, simply increasing the number of iterations
cannot further improve the accuracy of the positioning
results. The computational burden is much less onerous
than that of grid search method;
4. True triaxial compression test results show that the posi-
tioning results are consistent with the final failure modes
of the rock samples. Therefore, the proposed AE source
location method for layered rock provides an efective
way of studying the spatio-temporal evolution of layered
rock fracturing and its fracture mechanism under high
true triaxial compression stress.

rately reflect the anisotropic propagation velocity char-
acteristics of AE signals generated by microfracture in
layered rock;
2. A three-dimensional AE source location method for
layered rock is proposed based on simplex method and
the established anisotropic P-wave velocity model. The
iterative initial value exerts a relatively large influence
on the positioning accuracy of the proposed method,
while the iterative contraction length has relatively lit-
tle efect on the positioning accuracy. When the dis-
tance between the vertices of the initial simplex and the
center point is 1/2 of the minimum distance between
any two sensors and the contraction length is about
1/3 of the original side length of the tetrahedron, the
positioning efect is relatively good and stable;
3. For layered rocks with high anisotropy and heteroge-
neity, the location accuracy of the proposed method is
much higher than that of the traditional method (iso-
tropic P-wave velocity simplex method). In addition,
this method allows rapid convergence, as the number
of iterations increases, the localization error initially
decreases rapidly, but the rate of decrease slows down
as iterations continue. When the number of iterations
reaches 100, simply increasing the number of iterations
cannot further improve the accuracy of the positioning
results. The computational burden is much less onerous
than that of grid search method;
4. True triaxial compression test results show that the posi-
tioning results are consistent with the final failure modes
of the rock samples. Therefore, the proposed AE source
location method for layered rock provides an efective
way of studying the spatio-temporal evolution of layered
rock fracturing and its fracture mechanism under high
true triaxial compression stress.
